lines.text: Hi, I'm Sindy! Let's see how this video was made.
Videos go stale when the docs change. With plain text files, you fix a line and render again.
Coding agents can write them too. Checks tell them what they can't see.
It all starts with the script, one line per beat. The voice tool speaks each line and times every word.
The composition times every scene to them. Then HyperFrames renders it, with captions burned in.
Publish adds a poster and web captions, ready for your docs. And in CI, only changed episodes render again.
A project keeps only what's its own: its brand and lexicon, its episodes and checks.
Everything else, from my looks to the scenes, comes from the library.
All of it comes together in avatars.json. It casts me as the host, in my hoodie, and picks a theme, a format and the brand.
Grounding is the part I like best. What you see on screen must also be on the page around the video.
Let's make one. Run avatars new episode with a name, and out comes a working episode.
It holds three files: the script, the scenes in index.html, and a little HyperFrames config.
Then fixture voice fakes the timings, so you can lay out scenes now.
Fixture voice needs no speech model, and it's instant. It's made for layout work and tests.
The real voice runs a speech model on your CPU. Each line is cached, so only changed lines are voiced again.
Now for the real voice. It takes a few seconds per line, so let's skip ahead.
Then check loads the episode, and prints the chapters and lines.
Zero errors, zero warnings. It's ready to render!
To recap: an episode is two files you write, check guards what's on screen, and CI renders only what changed.
That's the whole tour! In the next one, I'll try on a new look. See you there!
